title: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
summary: LSA Secrets covers credential material that Windows stores in the SECURITY registry hive for the Local Security Authority, most often passwords belonging to service accounts and scheduled tasks, plus keys used by other system components. Reading this data requires SYSTEM level access, and the usual routes are saving the hive with a registry command, reading it from memory, or using a tool that talks to the same system interfaces. The secrets are attractive because service accounts frequently hold elevated rights and their passwords are rarely rotated, giving the adversary a stable and quiet foothold. Detection rests on registry hive export commands, unusual access to the SECURITY key, and process behaviour consistent with memory reading. Because system processes legitimately read this hive during startup, timing relative to a command line or an interactive session is the differentiator.

beginner.definition: LSA secrets are stored passwords that Windows keeps for services and system tasks. They live in a protected area of the registry. This sub-technique means stealing those stored secrets. It is narrower than the parent because service and system account details are the main prize.
beginner.whyItMatters: Service accounts often hold high rights and rarely change their passwords. Stealing them can give an attacker a stable and quiet way back in. These accounts may not be watched as closely as normal user accounts. The data is well protected, so reading it shows an attacker already holds strong access. Knowing this helps you decide which accounts need attention first.
howItWorks: Windows stores passwords for services and system tasks in a protected registry area.
Only a process running as SYSTEM can read that area in the normal way.
The attacker saves the SECURITY registry hive to a file on disk.
Alternatively, a tool reads the same secrets directly from memory.
The file or memory content is processed elsewhere to reveal the passwords.
Those passwords are then used to reach services and other systems.
beginner.example: Think of an office where each cleaner has a master key kept in a locked cupboard. Only the building manager may open that cupboard. A thief who becomes the manager for one night copies every key inside instead of taking one. All the keys go back, so nothing looks missing. LSA secrets are that cupboard, and the service accounts are the keys inside it.
takeaways: Service account passwords are the main target of this collection behaviour.
Registry hive exports and unusual SECURITY key access are the artefacts.
Rotate service account passwords if you suspect they were exposed.

objectives: Explain what LSA secrets are and which accounts they usually describe.
Describe the access level required to read the SECURITY registry hive.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the credential dumping parent.
Identify registry and memory artefacts linked to secret extraction.
Explain why unrotated service account passwords make this so valuable.
